name: The romantic revolt versus the rationalistic revolt
plain_explanation: Russell divides nineteenth-century rebellion against tradition into two families: a 'romantic' kind that prizes will, passion, and violence over reasoning and eventually feeds nationalism and fascism, and a 'rationalistic' kind that keeps faith with argument and science and eventually feeds Marxism and Soviet communism.
precise_definition: Two divergent lines of revolt against eighteenth-century tradition, both descended from the French Revolution and its immediate philosophical precursors: the romantic line (Byron, unphilosophically; Schopenhauer and Nietzsche, philosophically; culminating politically in Mussolini and Hitler) which emphasizes will over intellect, is impatient of chains of reasoning, glorifies certain kinds of violence, and allies with nationalism; and the rationalistic line (the French revolutionary philosophers, the English philosophical radicals, Marx) which remains committed to argument and, in Marx, to science.
why_it_mattered: It is the chapter's organizing framework and the reason Russell arranges the following chapters (Hegel, Byron, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Marx) as he does; it lets him treat wildly different figures -- a poet, a pessimist metaphysician, and a political economist -- as expressions of the same historical crisis of nineteenth-century rationalism.
historical_origin: Both currents are traced by Russell to the French Revolution and the philosophers who immediately preceded it.
associated_philosopher: Bertrand Russell (as historian's framework), exemplified by Byron/Schopenhauer/Nietzsche vs. Bentham/Marx
examples: Byron's 'Titanic cosmic self-assertion' as an unphilosophical form of the romantic revolt
Marx's scientific socialism as the mature form of the rationalistic revolt
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell traces the romantic line forward to Mussolini and Hitler and the rationalistic line forward to Soviet Russia, making this taxonomy the spine of the rest of Book Three, Part II.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly tied to the rise of Fascism and of Soviet communism as the twentieth-century political expressions of the two currents.
